title: DIY Project Based Learning for Math and Science
guide: Four big ideas from Wolpert-Gawron.
article:
My Book Share is DIY Project Based Learning for Math and Science by Heather Wolpert-Gawron (2016), an award-winning middle school teacher and Edutopia blogger. I am training to teach physics and Earth and space science, and I chose this book because I want my students doing science rather than only reading about it.

What follows covers four big ideas from the book, the key terms behind them, what each looks like in a real classroom, and three questions for discussion.

title: A line or a story?
guide: Is your current unit a line, or a story?
bullets: Disneyland vs. Six Flags: the story starts in line
Build the unit like a story.
article:
Wolpert-Gawron opens with a comparison that is hard to shake. At Disneyland, a ride's story begins the moment you step into line, with the walls, ceiling, and even the ground building toward it. At Six Flags, she jokes, the décor needs some serious work (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 3).

She admits she once taught disconnected daily lessons that never added up to a story. Project Based Learning, or PBL, is the Disneyland version: every lesson lives inside one story about a problem that has to be solved. Is your current unit a line, or a story?

title: Idea 1: A unit, not a project
guide: PBL runs the whole unit, start to finish.
bullets: "PBL is the act of learning through identifying a real world problem and developing its solution." (p. 2)
Assigning a project ≠ Project Based Learning (p. 7)
article:
The first idea is that PBL is a unit, not a project. The author's elevator speech: "PBL is the act of learning through identifying a real world problem and developing its solution" (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 2). Students show what they learn throughout the unit, not just at the end.

She draws a hard line between assigning a project and doing Project Based Learning (p. 7). An assigned project is an assessment tacked on at the end. PBL is the whole unit, with every lesson, exploration, piece of research, and presentation driven by one driving question.

title: How the story gets built
guide: Entry event, role play, authentic audience, heuristic tasks.
article:
Every unit in the book uses the same moves. An entry event hooks students into the problem. In the Galapagos Unit, an eighth grader films a video as the head of the Smithsonian, inviting seventh grade "explorers" to research an island and decide which species to save. In role play, students become doctors, inventors, field scientists, or theme park engineers. Their work goes to an authentic audience: a board, a principal, local STEM professionals, or other classes.

She also borrows A. J. Juliani's distinction. Algorithmic tasks follow one set path to one answer. Heuristic tasks take trial and error, and PBL lives there (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, pp. 4-5).

title: Idea 1 in practice
guide: Same skills as a worksheet, with somebody waiting on the answer.
bullets: HS Physics: Can your coaster carry a marble through a loop without falling off at the top?
article:
In an elementary roller coaster unit from teachers Emily Cruz and Melanie Valencia, children build coasters from foam tubing, marbles, and tape, adding a curve, a hill, then a loop, and recording why each trial worked or failed (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 80). In a middle school Invention Unit, students pitch a fix for an everyday problem at home.

In my high school physics class, I would make the coaster an energy unit. Can your coaster carry a marble through a loop without falling off at the top? Students predict in PhET's Energy Skate Park, build, film trials in slow motion, revise, and pitch to a "park safety board" of other teachers. Somebody is waiting on the answer.

title: An invention starts with a problem
guide: Needs analysis before the pitch.
bullets: Needs analysis: 3 to 5 problems in each major space
Jacob's Smart Drawer: a floor sensor opens the drawer
Rube Goldberg analysis: identify each step
article:
The Invention Unit includes a real student idea. Jacob calls it the Smart Drawer: if your hands are full, or a drawer is hard to open, you step on a floor pad and a sensor opens it for you.

Before anyone pitches, students walk through their homes and list three to five problems in each major space, which gives them somewhere to start. She also has them break a Rube Goldberg machine down into its steps. The purpose is to study sequence, and nobody has to build another machine (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, pp. 36-39, 79). I would run the same routine before asking my physics students to design a solution.

title: What students actually produced
guide: Assess the failed trial, not just the loop.
bullets: Trial notes explain what worked and why
article:
These photographs from the book show the student work behind the coaster unit. Students marked the track dimensions and labeled potential and kinetic energy (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 87). The teaching directions ask them to document each trial and explain why it worked or didn't (p. 80).

That documentation is what I would want to assess. A loop that works is fun to watch, but I would also want the student to explain a run that failed, point to the change they made, and show what happened on the next trial. My high school version remains a proposal. These elementary classroom examples are already in the book.

title: Idea 2: Design toward what you love
guide: Passion first, then standards, then fill the gaps.
article:
The second idea is to design toward what you love, then backplan to the standards. The author calls standards-first planning "a stinky model." Her three steps: design toward your interests and those of your students, look back at the standards, and fill in the gaps.

Enthusiasm, she argues, is "trickle down." A bored teacher means bored students. She calls this a teacher's maker movement: students make products, so teachers should make curriculum. When one teacher can't reach every standard, she recommends a cross-curricular partner. The Galapagos Unit came from her work with a seventh grade science teacher.

title: The checklist is a contract
guide: Show students where the unit is going.
article:
A pacing checklist keeps it from turning into chaos. It lists assignments and deadlines and goes to students, parents, and administrators on day one. She backplans from the final presentation date and leaves a few rows empty on purpose.

The checklist works as a contract. The teacher promises not to wing it, and students promise to plan ahead. "The mystery defeats achievement" (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 9).

In my physics class, an empty row might become a reteach day when students still think heavier objects fall faster, or a second build day if every coaster fails the loop. The schedule bends to what students still need.

title: The actual pacing checklist
guide: Students can see how the work fits together.
bullets: Design, cost analysis, then business letter
Empty boxes leave room for adjustments
article:
This is the actual Invention Unit checklist, with a date assigned, an assignment, and a deadline for each task (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 34). The order matters. The needs analysis comes before the problem statement, and the design and cost analysis come before the final business letter and presentation, so students can see how the pieces fit together.

The author also advises leaving some empty boxes for the teacher's own assignments or for students' individual goals. In my class, I would fill those when a quick check tells me we need another lesson or another trial.

title: Passion first vs. backward design
guide: Hook first. Check the standards before day one.
bullets: Steps 2 and 3 are the backward design
E&SS example: an air quality unit
article:
Backward design starts with learning goals and evidence of learning before any activities (Wiggins & McTighe, 2005). Wolpert-Gawron owns her departure: "Call me bass-ackward, but I don't design projects around the Common Core Standards" (2016, p. 7).

Look closer, though, and her steps two and three are backward design. She just puts the hook first. The tension is real. Passion can hook students, but skip step three and you get a fun project that misses the standards.

For Earth and space, I am drafting an air quality unit that starts with the air in my students' own town, then checks the standards and fills the holes before day one.

title: Idea 3: Communication is the content
guide: STEM students write the genres real professionals write.
bullets: "If it doesn't exist outside of school, then it isn't worthy enough to be taught within school." (p. 10)
Lab report, problem statement, business letter, executive summary
article:
The third idea: communication is the content. The author quotes her earlier book: "If it doesn't exist outside of school, then it isn't worthy enough to be taught within school" (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 10). Students write the genres STEM professionals write.

In the Genius Unit, students play doctors writing a lab report to a patient's family. In the Invention Unit, they write a problem statement, a short, researched case that a problem is real with three to five research questions, and a business letter asking a company to fund their invention. The Galapagos and Theme Park units end in an executive summary, a short pitch to a busy decision maker.

title: A student writes to a real reader
guide: Specific reader, specific request, evidence required.
chapter: Excerpt: Kevin Y. letter, Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, pp. 53-54
article:
Kevin's business letter is another student artifact worth a close look (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, pp. 53-54). He describes an invention he calls the Dust Mite, a flying vacuum, and asks a company to fund it. I like that students write to a specific reader with a specific request.

I wouldn't take his performance claims on faith, though. In physics, we would ask whether the design could actually lift its own weight and still power the vacuum. That question gives the next investigation a reason to exist, and it gives Kevin something concrete to revise.

title: Writing with numbers
guide: Numbers as evidence; BIRAC as the pitch outline.
bullets: Writing with numeracy (Ch. 2; Part II, p. 120)
BIRAC: Background, Issues, Recommendations, Analysis, Consequences (p. 82)
article:
Writing with numeracy teaches students to use numbers correctly as evidence, guided by a reference sheet of rules such as spelling out a number that begins a sentence (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 120).

BIRAC is an engineering-style outline for the Theme Park executive summary (p. 82): Background poses the question, Issues names obstacles, then Recommendations, Analysis of the evidence, and Consequences if the board says yes or no.

The Invention Unit's break-even analysis adds real math. Cost is C = vx + F, variable cost times units plus fixed cost. Revenue is R = px, price times units. Students graph both lines in Desmos and find where they cross.

title: Assess writing quickly
guide: The one doing the work is the one doing the learning.
article:
Each unit ends with a tip for grading writing quickly. One: focus feedback on one skill at a time, not a "bloody explosion of red pen." Two: use an oral feedback sheet, where the student takes the notes, because isn't the one doing the work the one doing the learning? Three: use feedback symbols. Four: comment rather than correct, as in "In your math assignment, I see three equations that do not add up." Five: train peers to give the first round of feedback.

In physics, I would write "One of your forces points the wrong way" instead of circling a wrong sign on an acceleration. The student does the thinking.

title: Idea 3 in practice
guide: Same content, explained to somebody who needs it.
bullets: Physics: lab report as an engineer's memo
article:
In middle school math, the break-even analysis gives students a reason to write and graph linear equations. In biology, the Galapagos executive summary turns natural selection and biodiversity into a funding argument.

In my air quality unit, students could pull real readings from the EPA's AirNow site, write them up with the numeracy rules, and present a BIRAC summary to the school board on protecting students on poor air days. In physics, a lab report written as an engineer's memo to a client is still a lab report. It just has an audience now.

title: Invented creature, evidence-based explanation
guide: Defend the design with habitat evidence.
article:
This student-created marine torguana comes from the Galapagos Unit (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, pp. 64-66). The creature is invented, but students must tie its design to the island's real habitat. Their explorers' journal covers the habitat, animal facts, and theories about why the species is disappearing, and they finish by pitching a protection plan.

I would ask students to defend one feature of their creature with evidence about its environment. The drawing is an inviting way in. The explanation is where I learn whether the science holds up.

title: Idea 4: Teach them to be teachers
guide: Students write the tests too.
bullets: "Teaching is the highest form of understanding." (Ch. 5, p. 89)
article:
The fourth idea: teach them to be teachers. The final unit rests on a line credited to Aristotle: "Teaching is the highest form of understanding" (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 89). Students teach a topic they love with a lesson plan and activity, then write a persuasive letter pitching it to an administrator as a new elective.

Throughout the book, students also write assessments using Costa's Levels of Questioning: input (recall, define, list), process (compare, infer, sequence), and output (predict, hypothesize, evaluate, create). She dramatizes them with a two-pound weight, a twenty-five-pound weight, and a hundred-pound barbell she can't lift. A test of all level one questions only checks memorization.

title: What would those questions sound like?
guide: Costa's levels, made concrete.
bullets: Book example: Shakespeare's seven ages. Agree or disagree? Why? (p. 97)
Level 2: Compare friction-force versus normal-force graphs.
Level 3: Design a fair test of contact area.
chapter: Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 97. Physics questions: my adaptation.
article:
Concrete questions make the levels clearer. The book asks whether you agree with Shakespeare that people have seven ages in their lifetime, and why, as one of its level three examples (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 97).

My own adaptation translates the framework into friction. Level one asks what the coefficient of friction means. Level two asks students to compare two force graphs and explain what the slopes tell us. Level three asks them to design a fair test of whether contact area changes sliding friction. These physics questions are mine, not the book's. I would review the questions students write before they hand them to classmates.

title: Students write the tests
guide: Able to Teach This Topic is the required top rubric level.
bullets: Top rubric level: "Able to Teach This Topic" (p. 98)
Collaboration constitution: peers grade only on rules they wrote (Ch. 4)
article:
Four tools put assessment in students' hands. In the Genius Unit, each student reads an article and builds a ten-question Google Forms quiz for classmates, mixing levels and formats. Students rewrite the district rubric in their own words, and the top score must be "Able to Teach This Topic" (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 98).

During presentations, a backchannel lets the audience type questions into a shared document, and the author grades them by counting level two and three questions (p. 103). Finally, teams write a collaboration constitution at the start of a unit and may grade each other only on the rules they wrote.

title: Students put the rubric into their own words
guide: Able to Teach is the top score.
bullets: "Every piece of the prompt is included clearly"
article:
This student-created rubric appears in the book (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 101). At the top level, the students wrote, "Able to Teach." One descriptor reads, "Great evidence, quotes." Another reads, "Every piece of the prompt is included clearly." The students know what those words mean because they helped write them.

For a physics explanation, I would ask the class what convincing evidence looks like. We would still need accurate physics and clear criteria, but students could help put those expectations into words they would actually use when reviewing a partner's work.

title: A real collaboration constitution
guide: Agree on language before you need it.
bullets: Write a way to address nonparticipation
Set realistic expectations for this class
article:
The collaboration constitution makes more sense once you see what students actually wrote (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, p. 85). This team agreed to answer messages within three hours and to talk through problems before asking the teacher to step in.

I wouldn't copy that three-hour deadline into my class. My students have different responsibilities and different access at home, so I would have them agree on something realistic. The assignment also asks students to write a sentence they can use when someone isn't participating, which gives them words for an awkward conversation before they need them.

title: Idea 4 in practice
guide: A shared doc gives quiet students a voice.
bullets: ELA/History: teach a skill, score classmates' quizzes
Math: explain it so a peer can solve the next one
Physics: each lab group teaches one concept
article:
In ELA or history, students can teach a short skill lesson and score classmates' quizzes, which is real data analysis. In math, "Able to Teach" could mean explaining a solution well enough that a classmate can solve the next problem.

In my physics class, each lab group would teach one concept, such as friction, momentum, or energy transfer, and write a three-question quiz with one question at each Costa level. The backchannel helps too. Quieter students often have the best questions, and a shared document gives them a voice without raising a hand.

title: Where I'd push back
guide: PBL changes the teacher's job. The teacher still teaches.
bullets: Authentic work still needs a content check
Pair classroom stories with a framework (PBLWorks Gold Standard; Larmer et al., 2015)
article:
The book has limits. Published in 2016, it relies on tools like TodaysMeet, a backchannel site that shut down years ago, so a shared Google Doc or Canvas discussion should stand in.

The Teach Them to Be Teachers unit uses a multiple intelligences quiz and mentions learning styles, yet Pashler et al. (2008) found little evidence that matching instruction to learning styles improves learning. Keep the variety, drop the labels. Some brain science claims in the Genius Unit lab reports are shaky, so authentic work still needs a content check. Most evidence is teacher stories and student samples, so pair it with the PBLWorks Gold Standard (Larmer et al., 2015) and watch your own data. If quiz scores drop, add direct instruction. The teacher still has to teach.

title: A student sample can still need revision
guide: Credit the audience choice; still verify the science.
bullets: Thoughtful audience choice: recommend a second opinion
article:
The fictional patient report shows why that content check matters (Wolpert-Gawron, 2016, pp. 28-30). The student recommends a second opinion, a thoughtful choice for the audience. Elsewhere, though, the report makes claims about brain structure I would want students to verify.

I would use it as a revision example. Students can earn credit for strong communication choices while the class still asks whether the evidence supports the science.

title: Key terms
guide: The vocabulary of a PBL unit.
article:
The book's key terms, in one place:

A driving question is the real-world problem that anchors the whole unit. An entry event hooks students into it. An authentic audience is someone outside the teacher who needs the answer. Backplanning means setting the final date first and working backward on the pacing checklist. A problem statement is a short, researched case that a problem is real. BIRAC is the five-part outline for an executive summary. Costa's Levels of Questioning sort questions into input, process, and output. "Able to Teach This Topic" is the top rubric score, meaning a student understands the topic well enough to teach it.

title: Conclude with direction
guide: Four ideas to take into your classroom.
article: Four ideas are worth carrying forward. First, PBL is a unit, not a project, so build the whole story around a real problem. Second, design toward what you and your students love, then backplan to the standards and fill the gaps, using a checklist that shows everyone where the unit is headed. Third, in STEM, communication is the content. Give students real genres and real audiences, and use quick feedback tools so the grading doesn't bury you. Fourth, teach students to be teachers by having them write the questions, the rubrics, and the lessons.

title: Discussion questions
guide: Apply an idea from this Bookshare to your classroom.
questions: In this Bookshare, Wolpert-Gawron's planning order (design toward what you love, then look back at the standards, then fill the gaps) was compared with backward design. Choose a unit you will teach. Which order would you plan it in, and what would you put in the empty rows of your pacing checklist to keep it flexible? Explain how your choice connects to an idea from the presentation. Refer to one assignment shown in the actual Invention Unit checklist.

The presentation shared five ways to assess writing quickly and argued that in STEM, communication is the content. Pick one real-world genre from this Bookshare (problem statement, executive summary with BIRAC, business letter, or lab report) and describe how you would use it in your subject. Which feedback tip would you pair it with, and how does that tip shift who does the work?

The book insists that the top level of a rubric be called "Able to Teach This Topic." In addition to the approaches in the presentation (student-created quizzes, student-translated rubrics, backchanneling), what other way could students in your classroom prove they can teach a concept? What evidence would convince you, and what is one risk of the approach? Compare your proposal with one descriptor in the student-created rubric shown in this Bookshare.
article: Each of the three discussion questions asks you to carry an idea from this Book Share into your own classroom. The first concerns planning order and the empty rows of the pacing checklist. The second pairs a real-world genre with a feedback tip. The third asks what other ways students can prove they are able to teach.
